source_text: Sed iam tempus est, ut de Evangelii sententia disseratur. Dicebat, inquit evangelista Ioannes, Iesus ad Iudaeos eos qui crediderunt ei: Si vos manseritis in sermone meo, vere discipuli mei eritis; et cognoscetis veritatem, et veritas liberabit vos [n197] . Id est, Dominus noster Iesus loquebatur ad credentes sibi, ut de nulla saeculi nobilitate gaudentes, nec de Abrahae sibi semine gloriam vindicantes, niterentur et studerent virtutibus, et nullis post agnitio m Christi servire peccatis, ut veram libertatem conscientia gaudente retinerent, et spe certorum, id est aeternorum, vindicarentur a cupiditate aliorum omnium, quae propter fragilitatem sui, vana frequenter et falsa dicuntur. Tunc responderunt ei Iudaei, non intellegentes de qua Iesus libertate dixisset: Semen Abrahae sumus, et nemini servivimus umquam; quomodo tu dicis: Liberi eritis? [n198] Multis enim modis libertas appellari solet, ut in hoc loco sanctitas, ut resurrectio in Apostolo, ubi dicit creaturam liberari a servitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriae filiorum Dei [n199] ; ut libertas quae notior est, ad distinctionem dicitur servitutis. Eo autem nomine et libertas nuncupatur arbitrii. Dividantur ergo causae, ne res multum distantes confundantur nominis communione. Hic ergo non arbitrii libertatem Dominus dicit esse liberandam; sed illa integra permanente, convenit Iudaeos, ut accipientes indulgentiam liberentur a reatibus, et eam quae apud Deum maxima est, libertatem occupent, ut incipiant nihil debere criminibus. Denique sequitur Evangelista: Respondit eis Iesus: Amen, amen dico vobis, quoniam omnis qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati. Servus autem non manet in domo in aeternum; filius autem manet in aeternum. Si ergo Filius vos liberaverit, tunc vere liberi eritis [n200] .
pass_a_gloss: But already it is time that it be discussed about the sentence of the Gospel. Jesus was saying, says the evangelist John, to those Jews who had believed him: If you shall have remained in my speech, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will free you. That is, our Lord Jesus was speaking to those believing him, that rejoicing from no nobility of the age, nor claiming glory for themselves from the seed of Abraham, they should strive and study virtues, and after the recognition of Christ serve no sins, that they might retain true liberty with a rejoicing conscience, and by hope of certain things, that is eternal, be vindicated from desire of all other things, which on account of their fragility are frequently called vain and false. Then the Jews answered him, not understanding about which liberty Jesus had spoken: We are the seed of Abraham, and we have never served anyone; how do you say: You will be free? For liberty is accustomed to be named in many modes, as in this place holiness, as resurrection in the Apostle, where he says that the creature is freed from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God; as that liberty which is better known is said to the distinction of slavery. But by that name also the liberty of choice is named. Let therefore the cases be divided, lest things much distant be confused by a communion of name. Here therefore the Lord does not say that the liberty of choice is to be freed; but that remaining intact, he convenes the Jews, that receiving indulgence they may be freed from guilts, and occupy that liberty which is greatest with God, that they begin to owe nothing to charges. Finally the Evangelist follows: Jesus answered them: Amen, amen I say to you, that everyone who does sin is a slave of sin. But a slave does not remain in the house unto eternity; but a son remains unto eternity. If therefore the Son shall have freed you, then you will be truly free.

pass_b_english: It is now time to discuss the Gospel's statement. The evangelist John says: “Jesus said to the Jews who had believed in him, ‘If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free’” (John 8:31–32). That is, our Lord Jesus was telling those who believed in him not to rejoice in worldly nobility or claim glory from Abraham's descent, but to strive and labor for virtue and, after recognizing Christ, to serve no sins. They would thereby retain true freedom with a joyful conscience and, through hope in things that are certain, that is, eternal, be freed from desire for everything else, which because of its fragility is frequently called empty and false.

Then the Jews, not understanding what freedom Jesus meant, answered him: “We are Abraham's offspring and have never been anyone's slaves. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?” (John 8:33). “Freedom” is commonly used in many senses. Here it means holiness. In the apostle it means resurrection, when he says that creation is to be freed from slavery to corruption into the glorious freedom of God's children (Romans 8:21). In its better-known sense it is spoken of in contrast to slavery. The same name is also used for freedom of choice. Let us therefore distinguish the cases, so that things far apart are not confused because they share a name. Here the Lord does not say that freedom of choice needs to be set free. Rather, while it remains intact, he calls on the Jews to receive forgiveness and be freed from guilt, obtaining the freedom that is greatest in God's sight: to begin to owe no debt for crimes.

The evangelist continues: “Jesus answered them, ‘Amen, amen, I tell you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. If, then, the Son sets you free, you will be truly free’” (John 8:34–36).
